paragraphs.text: vv. 1–2. Blessed is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the ungodly, nor stood in the way of sinners, nor sat in the seat of the pestilent. But his will is in the law of the Lord, and on his law he will meditate day and night. Vat. B, p. 625, 1.

Blessed, then, is the one who longs for the things that truly are. But how can blessedness consist in the removal of evils? Abstaining from evils is common even to lifeless things and irrational animals. That is why he added: But his will is in the law of the Lord. This is natural only to a rational being, but [?] fleeing evils is also the beginning of taking up good things. For it says, “Turn away from evil, and do good.” On a ladder the first step up is leaving the ground, and in the same way the first step in progress toward God is separation from evil. In general, too, any kind of inactivity is easier than even an ordinary action. For example, “You shall not commit adultery, you shall not fornicate,” and the rest require of each person only inactivity and stillness. But “You shall love your neighbor,” and “Sell your possessions and give to the poor,” and “If anyone compels you to go one mile, go with him two” are already the deeds of a vigorous soul, and of athletes. — If he had set the perfect things before you at once, you would have shrunk from attempting them. As it is, he first accustoms you to easier things, so that you may venture on what follows. Just as some deeds are fit only for athletes, so we need a soul that is already vigorous to accomplish them. So marvel at the wisdom of the one who leads us toward perfection through easier and more attainable things. — The way of sinners may be said to be the devil. Whoever has come onto it must not remain there, according to the saying, “Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.” For whoever has not stood on it will come to the Lord, who said, “I am the way”; and whoever is on that way and runs toward the goal will win the prizes.
Of the ungodly: of those who do not know God.
On the seat: the practice of evil, which is passed on from one person to another.
But his will is in the law: plainly, the law of the Gospel.
He will meditate: in his deliberation.
v. 3. And he will be like the tree planted by the streams of waters, which will yield its fruit in its season, and its leaf will not fall, and in all that he does he will prosper.

In the divinely inspired Scripture, Christ is described as a tree. — Aquila rendered the word as “transplanted.” For he was rooted in the roots of the patriarchs and then transplanted, so that others too might share in his image, the image understood as transplanting. This is also said of the Savior's soul, which was transplanted from here into paradise. For he said to the thief: “Today you will be with me in the paradise of God.”
The streams of waters are the divine Scriptures, in which Christ can be found proclaimed everywhere.
You should understand the fruit of the tree as the right faith.

Its leaves are the fulfilment of the commandments. One of the saints used to say that the leaves are the humility of ascetics, which shelters their fruits and never falls. — He will prosper: for nothing done in accordance with God is unprofitable.
v. 4. Not so the ungodly, not so.
Some add the second “not so.” But the Hebrew does not double the expression, and none of the translators repeated the phrase.
v. 5. Therefore the ungodly will not rise up in judgment.
When he says that the ungodly will not rise, he means that they will rise to judgment, not to examination.
v. 6. For the Lord knows the way of the righteous, and the way of the ungodly will perish.

“Knows” stands for “honours,” as in God's words to Moses: “I know you above all, and you have found favour with me.” It should be noted as a general rule that only what is good is known by the Lord, and the way of the righteous is good. Moreover, the Lord knew those who are his, and he knew the way of the righteous, since he said, “I am the way.” — The way of the ungodly is the one travelled by those who speak evil of the Creator. They are like chaff blown away by the wind, and so they are not counted worthy of the resurrection in judgment, just as sinners are not counted worthy of the counsel of the righteous. The way of the righteous is worthy of God's knowledge, and so it is known by him; but the way of the ungodly will perish, because the Lord does not know it. — By saying that the way of the ungodly perishes, he corrected the notions of the heretics. On the basis of the words “but like the chaff which the wind drives from the face of the earth,” they supposed that the very substance of the ungodly vanishes into nonexistence. But when the way perishes, it is the ungodliness that ceases to exist, while those in whom it was found remain.

Argument. At the opening of the blessing it was laid down that one must not be ungodly. The second psalm then sets out what lies outside ungodliness, proclaiming the mystery of the Gospel in advance. In a way, then, the first psalm serves as a title for the second. There the psalm speaks of the birth in the flesh of Christ, who was born “today” for our sake (“today” being a part of time), yet who is always from the Father and in the Father, Son and God. It also speaks of [his] kingdom over those who had no king, who were counted among the nations because they did not serve God. Vat., p. 625, 1.
v. 3. Let us burst their bonds and cast their yoke away from us.

The nations are bound tight by their own sins and are not free. That is why Christ speaks these words, addressing either the angels who minister to him, or the Father and the Holy Spirit, or the apostles who serve the Gospel, and urging them to tear apart the nations' bonds. The peoples were bodily under the yoke of the law, which contains “statutes that were not good and ordinances that were not good.” But they are brought through Christ to the spiritual law, which has good statutes and ordinances, and so they lay aside the heavy yoke of the letter that kills. For the Savior says to the fellow-workers already mentioned, “Let us cast their yoke away from us,” that is, let us do this of our own accord, without waiting for those weighed down to plead with us. Or else, since he himself also came under the law (for it is written that he was circumcised and kept their Sabbaths), he means “from me and from those who obey,” or rather: out of our love for them, let us treat their yoke as our own burden and cast it away. These things, then, concern human beings, both those from the nations and those of the people.
v. 4. He who dwells in the heavens will laugh them to scorn, and the Lord will deride them.

The words “He who dwells in the heavens will laugh them to scorn” refer to the kings of the earth. The Lord in heaven will laugh them to scorn because their minds are set on earthly things and they have not understood the wisdom of the Savior's incarnation. And he will deride the rulers too. It was fitting for the Son of God to say: Even if the nations raged and the peoples devised vain things, let us burst the bonds of the one and cast off the yoke of the other, since they no longer readily accept healing. For they refused to come inside the sacred dragnet, of which it is written: “The kingdom of heaven is like a net cast into the sea.”
v. 5. Then he will speak to them in his wrath.

God's wrath is a painful punishment given for the benefit of the one who has sinned. But at the time of judgment all the enemies of the saving Word will experience the wrath of God and be troubled by his anger. He did not say, “He will punish them,” but “He will speak to them in his wrath.” For he did not punish those who repented, as in the case of the Ninevites. “For God threatens for the sake of salvation,” he said, and he sent Jonah to the Ninevites.
v. 7. Today I have begotten you.
“Today” is a name for “always.”
v. 8. Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance.
The devil showed the Savior the kingdoms of these nations and their glory in a moment of time.
v. 12. Lay hold of instruction.
Instruction is the moderation of the passions, which naturally comes from the practical life. And the practical life is a spiritual teaching that purifies the passionate part of the soul.
v. 2. Lord, why have those who afflict me multiplied? Vat., p. 625, 2.
Those who make progress have many who afflict them.
v. 4. But you, Lord, are my helper, my glory, and the one who lifts up my head.

The mind is lifted up at the moment it applies itself to the manifold wisdom of God. — God is the glory of the saint, and everyone whose glory is God is lifted up by him. The “head” means the elevation of the soul. The head of a person of tall stature is raised above the heads of lesser people, which lie below it. In the same way, when the soul of the blessed man rises up, his head is lifted up, with God working together with it.
v. 5. And he heard me from his holy mountain.
Consider whether the Only-begotten could be the holy mountain from which God will hear.
v. 8. Arise, Lord; save me, my God; for you have struck all who are hostile to me without cause; you have broken the teeth of sinners.

God has a particular disposition toward each person. Those for whom he has arisen he also saves, but those who are hostile without cause he strikes. — “Hostile without cause” is like the saying, “They hated me without cause.” The teeth of sinners broken by the Lord are like those spoken of in the sayings “There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth” and “The teeth of the one who eats the sour grape will be set on edge.”
v. 1. For the end; among the psalms; a song of David. Vat., p. 625, 2.

Argument. In the Septuagint many psalms bear the title “For the end,” while the other translators give equivalent expressions in its place. It is therefore worth tracing, as far as we can, the meaning signified by the phrase. We should recognize that every art and science has its end, toward which the one who genuinely pursues that art or science strives; in the same way the rational nature must also have an end. And this end is to be made alive in Christ, according to what the most wise Paul says in the First Epistle to the Corinthians: “For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive, but each in his own order.” — By saying “in his own order,” he does not describe a single end for everyone. It is likely that each will be made alive according to the worth of his deeds, reaching that end either without torment or after punishments. And Christ, having made alive in himself all who die in Adam, reigns over those who have been made alive. — We think, therefore, that the psalms titled “For the end” point to some sense of the end and call those who understand what is said toward it. — For everyone who competes, victory too is an end. There are many partial victories and ends, as Paul shows when he says at one point, “In all these things we are more than conquerors through him who loved us,” and at another, “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith. From now on there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, will award to me on that day, and not only to me but also to all who have loved his appearing.”
v. 2. When I called, the God of my righteousness heard me; in affliction you made room for me. Vat., p. 626, 1.

He heard me not after I called, but while I was calling. — It is when we come to recognize the reasons for afflictions and temptations that we are most enlarged. The prophet calls as a man, and because he calls, he is heard by the God of his righteousness, meaning the righteousness of the one speaking, and for this reason he is brought into a broad place in times of affliction. Yet compared with God such a person is still below. For the eyes of the Lord are lofty, but man is lowly and needs God's pity.
v. 3. Sons of men, how long will you be heavy of heart?

Someone may think that “sons of men” is a periphrasis, since the Greeks also commonly use this figure of speech, saying “sons of the Achaeans” and the like. — Here we learn that evil is heavy by nature. That is why the Lord, when he comes into Egypt, is said to sit on a light cloud. And a light cloud is a rational nature filled with all virtue and knowledge.
v. 4. And know that the Lord has made his holy one wonderful.

Know, then, you who trust in multitudes, that he has made wonderful the one who trusts in him. — In Psalm 15 David prophesies about Christ that he is the true holy one, and the apostles bear witness about him, having understood the words, “Nor will you let your holy one see corruption.” But the verse can also be taken as teaching about every holy person. Believing and knowing are not the same thing, just as believing the truth is not the same as knowing the truth, and believing God is not the same as knowing God. Accordingly the Savior says to the apostles, who had already believed: “If you abide in my word, you are truly my disciples, and you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free.” For as Isaiah says, “Unless you believe, you will not understand.” And David says, “I believed, therefore I spoke.” And the words “Be still and know that I am God” show that knowing differs from believing, for they were not spoken to unbelievers. The verse also shows what kind of knowledge one will need to receive, [and] how the holy ones were made wonderful by God, being led to the wonders of the ineffable mysteries and the holy contemplations. Μεγάλη [?] BB, p. 560.
v. 5. Be angry, and do not sin.
He urges us not to assent to the mental image, and not to confirm our anger by carrying it into action.
v. 6. Offer a sacrifice of righteousness, and hope in the Lord.
The sacrifice of righteousness is the rational soul's freedom from passion, offered to God; and hope is the good expectation of true knowledge.
v. 7. The light of your face has been stamped upon us, Lord.

The angels continually behold the face of God, but human beings see the light of his face. For the face of the Lord is the spiritual contemplation of all things that have come to be on earth, and the light of his face is a partial knowledge of these same things. So, according to the wise woman of Tekoa, “David was like an angel of God, knowing all things on earth.”
v. 8. You have put gladness into my heart, from the fruit of grain and wine and oil.

In many places Scripture promises these things to the saints and threatens sinners with the loss of them. It means, of course, the intelligible things and not the things perceived by the senses. Some people thought these promises were bad because they seemed so small, and chose to worship another god they had invented themselves. But each soul that partakes of the better things is sanctified and gains the strength to accomplish the works that fall to it. And Paul carried these things over into the age to come as well: “Let no one judge you in food or drink, or with regard to a festival or a new moon or Sabbaths, which are a shadow of the things to come.” — Grain and wine and oil multiply sinners, but the gladness of God gladdens the righteous.
v. 1. For the end, concerning her who inherits. Vat., p. 626, 1.
Christ's inheritance is the rational nature.
v. 8. I will worship toward your holy temple in fear of you.

Christ is God's holy temple, because God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself. — In the fear of God everyone turns away from evil, and in the fear of the Lord one worships the temple, which is Christ. For he says, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.”
v. 9. Lord, lead me in your righteousness because of my enemies.
In the righteousness of the practical life, in Christ. — Of my enemies: clearly the spiritual ones. For many plot against the soul that loves God, envying its progress toward God.
v. 10. For there is no truth in their mouth; their heart is vain.
The first clause means there is no truth, or no Christ. Perhaps the second refers to [?] their plotting. Their throat is an open grave: it is filled with dead works.
v. 11. Judge them, O God; let them fall from their schemes; according to the multitude of their ungodly deeds cast them out, for they have embittered you, Lord.

God does not cast anyone out of his own accord. For it says, “Those who remove themselves far from you will perish.” Cast them out, then, from the multitude of their ungodly deeds. For he says, “They devised all these schemes against me, opposing my progress toward God.” Those who persecute the soul that does what is pleasing to God embitter God and are plainly fighting against him. — Cast them out of ungodliness by making them godly. — It is blessedness to fall away from every counsel.
v. 12. And let all who hope in you be glad in you; they will rejoice forever, and you will dwell among them.

Once the plotters have been destroyed, there is gladness, since you dwell in them forever. How could anyone fail to rejoice when God is present with him, living and walking in him as in his own temple? In the same way, to be far from God, taken captive by sin, deserves lamentation. The goal of all good things is to receive an inheritance and to have God dwelling within as one's portion.
v. 13. As with a shield of your favour you have crowned us.
Our crown, he says, is the grace that rewards our labours, which [?] fences us about as with a shield.
vv. 2–3. Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger, nor discipline me in your wrath. Have mercy on me, Lord, for I am weak; heal me, Lord, for my bones are troubled. Vat., p. 626, 2.

Anger is an impulse of desire in a gentle soul, chiefly toward retaliation [?]. So he says: Even if anger rebukes more harshly and wrath disciplines more swiftly, I, because of my weakness, need your mercy and need to be rebuked by some other treatment that does not bring such great pains. He wishes not to be rebuked by God's anger and not to be disciplined in his wrath, but to receive mercy, since he is weak, and to be healed of the trouble in his bones and in his soul. — Symmachus: “in rage,” “without delay.”
v. 6. For in death there is no one who remembers you. Vat., p. 627, 1.
No one who remembers the Life, which said, “I am the life,” is in death.
v. 7. Every night I will wash my bed.
An exhortation to weep while praying at night.
v. 11. Let all my enemies be put to shame and greatly troubled.

Demons work lawlessness always; humans do so not always; angels neither always nor not always, that is, never. — Falling away from wicked schemes is no evil for the one who falls away, since he does not reach their wicked end; just as it is not good to fail to reach the end of better things.
v. 5. If I have repaid those who repaid me with evil, then let me fall empty before my enemies. Vat., p. 627, 1.

The empty person is the one who cannot say, “From his fullness we have all received, grace upon grace.” That is why such people are also called reeds: they nourish within themselves the beasts of which it is said, “Rebuke the beasts of the reed.” And Job says, “The devil sleeps beside all kinds of trees, beside papyrus and rush and reed; for he is king of all that are in the waters.”
v. 6. Then let the enemy pursue my soul and overtake it.
So that I would become earthly instead of heavenly.
v. 10. Let the wickedness of sinners come to an end, and you will guide the righteous.
If the wickedness of sinners comes to an end, the righteous man keeps his way straight, since they no longer make war on him.
v. 13. If you do not turn back, he will burnish his sword.
The intelligible sword is the spiritual word, which separates the soul from the body, or from vice, or from ignorance.
v. 14. He has prepared instruments of death; he has made his arrows for those who are burning.
Those who are burning are those who receive the fiery arrows of the devil.
v. 17. And his injustice will come down upon the top of his head.
Here the top of the head signifies the mind, since according to Solomon the crown of grace, which is wisdom, is bound upon the top of the head.
v. 1. For the end, concerning the winepresses. Vat., p. 467, 2.
Punitive and retributive.

Eusebius. Here it says “for the end” because what is prophesied in this psalm has come to pass at the consummation of the ages. It says “concerning the winepresses” because of the peoples established throughout the whole earth and the churches of God, which Scripture regularly calls winepresses in allegory. In ancient times, when there was a single people called Israel, that people was called a vineyard. The temple among them was the tower, and the altar before the temple was the winepress vat, according to Isaiah's prophecy. But now Scripture speaks not of one winepress but of many, because of the many altars established throughout the whole earth through Christ in his churches. That is why Psalm 83, which is also titled “Concerning the winepresses,” foretells many altars, a great many dwellings and many courts. These plainly signify the altars set up throughout the whole earth in the churches of God, and so this psalm too bears the title “Concerning the winepresses.”

Origen. The eightieth psalm is also titled “For the end, concerning the winepresses, of Asaph,” and it begins, “Rejoice in God our helper.” And in Psalm 83 you will find the title “Concerning the winepresses.” Alongside these, let us consider the passages about Noah planting a vine; Jacob's blessing on Judah, “Binding his colt to the vine”; and his blessing on Issachar, who saw that rest was good and the land was rich, put his shoulder to the work, and became a farmer. Uzziah too was a farmer and had vinedressers in the hill country. And the wife of every righteous man is like a vine flourishing on the sides of his house, which produces wine that gladdens the human heart. Ecclesiastes says, “He planted vineyards, he dug a winepress.” And Solomon says, “And may your winepresses overflow with wine.”
v. 3. Because of your enemies, to destroy the enemy and avenger.

Origen. As an enemy, Satan compels us to sin; as an avenger, he punishes those handed over to him. So, after making Hymenaeus and Alexander blasphemers, he in turn disciplined them for their blasphemies against God.
v. 6. You made him a little lower than the angels; you crowned him with glory and honour.

Eusebius. You will see how the God of all crowned man with glory and honour from the fact that of man alone is it recorded that God said: "Let us make man according to our image and according to likeness"; and God made man, according to the image of God he made him. He also counted him worthy of appearances of himself, and granted divine converse to one clothed in flesh: at times through angels, at other times appearing to the saints himself, in his own person, and speaking to them. Besides this, he made him a sharer in the divine Spirit and in heavenly power, so that he could foretell what was to come, heal every kind of disease, and even raise the dead, as the prophets and apostles are recorded to have done. And if to all that has been said you add the incarnate dispensation of the only-begotten Son of God, you will see how it is said: "You crowned him with glory and honour", that is, man.
v. 1. I will give thanks to you, Lord, with my whole heart; I will tell of all your wonders. Vatic. p. 628, 1.

Others say that the present psalm is sung to him, not about him. On this view the prophet gives thanks on behalf of human nature, and says that it is the mark of the perfect to dedicate their whole heart to God: "For you shall love," it says, "the Lord your God with your whole heart," and so on. This is what "with my whole heart" now indicates. And what he does, having foreseen with prophetic eyes the things to come, he also recounts. He makes his hearers partners in his thanksgiving, possessing joy, the fruit of the Spirit, and recounting the wonders of God in lofty contemplations.
v. 6. You rebuked the nations, and the ungodly one perished; you blotted out their name for ever and ever.

For the sake of human nature, which was held under his tyranny, you laid so bitter a punishment on him. You rebuked the nations, that is, you handed down the divine teachings to them through the apostles and the teachers who came after them. When the nations received these teachings, [the ungodly one] perished, for he no longer had people worshipping him in error. In this way Paul and Barnabas rebuked the Lycaonians when they tried to offer sacrifice, saying: "Men, what are you doing? We too are men of like passions with you, turning you from these vain things." Paul also rebuked the Galatians: "O foolish Galatians, who has bewitched you, before whose eyes Jesus Christ was publicly portrayed among you as crucified?" So too the Corinthians: "It is actually reported that there is sexual immorality among you, and of a kind not even named among the gentiles." So his name has been blotted out for ever. For every rite of people now [?] who are ignorant of the mysteries of godliness has been extinguished. Such too is the saying: "The way of the ungodly will perish."
v. 8. But the Lord remains for ever; he has prepared his throne for judgement.
He has shown his power not only in the present life. In the life to come he will also show all people his awesome tribunal, as he judges and gives to each what they deserve.
v. 9. And he himself will judge the world in righteousness; he will judge the peoples with uprightness.

By "the world", that is, the inhabited world, you are to understand the church, which is inhabited by both the Father and the Son, as it is said: "I and my Father will come and make our dwelling with him." By "the peoples" you are to understand those outside the church, or those of the circumcision. For all who have sinned under the law will be judged by the law, while those who sinned without the law perish without the law. So those whose deeds are blameworthy and whose mindset is ungodly must fear such a judge.
v. 13. He did not forget the prayer of the poor.
What kind of prayer was this? It was the one made with laments and wailing, containing, as it were, a plea about the evils that held them fast.
v. 14. You who lift me up from the gates of death.
This is so that the gates of Hades may not prevail against him either. These gates are the vices that drag one down to the depths of Hades.
v. 16. The nations are caught fast in the corruption they wrought; in this snare which they hid, their own foot was taken.

Since virtue is called incorruption, as in the saying "Grace be with those who love our Lord in incorruption," the vice opposed to it may fittingly be called corruption and decay. At any rate it is said: "If anyone corrupts, God will corrupt him." And in the prophet: "Because of uncleanness you have been corrupted with corruption."
v. 17. The Lord is known by the judgements he carries out.
Sometimes a person is led along by judgements as well, and so comes to recognize the Lord.
v. 18. Let sinners be turned back into Hades, all the nations that forget God.

Sinners are turned back into Hades so that they may see the soul of Jesus going down and coming up again. For those who were waiting for it were looking outward, as it were: first the sinners among us, then the nations. Why did the nations forget the Lord? Forgetting comes after knowing. From this the saying also becomes clear: "I planted you as a fruitful vine, wholly true; how have you turned to bitterness, you alien vine?"
v. 28, 29. His mouth is full of cursing... He sits in ambush with the rich in secret places.
The righteous man blesses the Lord at all times, but the sinner sits in ambush.

v. 30–32. He lies in wait in secret like a lion in his den; he lies in wait to seize the poor man, to seize the poor man by dragging him into his snare. He will humble him; he will stoop and fall when he has gained mastery over the poor.

Just as a lion turns its eye this way and that in search of prey, so he devises schemes of plunder and greed night and day. Yet he will stoop and fall. He drags by means of thought, but he seizes through sin carried out in action.
v. 33. Do not forget the poor.
If the Lord forgot the poor, then the Lord knew the poor.
v. 34. For he said in his heart: "He will not seek it out."
Even if he reasons this way ten thousand times, you see. This is how it must be understood.
v. 36. Break the arm of the sinner and the wicked man.

A sinner is one who sins out of love of pleasure and licentiousness; a wicked man is one who does evil deliberately. — By "arm" he means the soul that has done wicked things. Breaking the arm wipes out sins, and being set free from sins is the benefit of having one's arm broken. This is how I too am convinced that God punishes.
v. 37, 38. The Lord is king for ever and for ever and ever; you nations will perish from his land. The Lord has heard the desire of the poor.

For the Lord must reign through the ages until the Lord has heard the desire of the poor, until he puts all his enemies as a footstool under his feet. His kingdom is the contemplation of all the ages that have been and will be, and through this contemplation even enemies become friends. The land of the Lord is the contemplation of the ages that have been. And the kingdom, we say, is this: the Lord hears the desire at the moment when he gives the soul that desired it what it desired.
v. 4. His eyes look upon the poor; his eyelids examine the sons of men. Vatic. p. 629, 2.

If the eyes of the Lord look upon the poor, let us become poor, so that the eyes of the Lord may look upon us. And if the rich are not poor, the eyes of the Lord do not look upon the rich. — When you hear from holy scripture that God is in the heavens, or that he sojourns, or that he is within the veil, do not imagine any boundaries or local dwellings, or movements, ascents and departures. Our nature is beggarly, and the Holy Spirit speaks to it in the way it is able to hear. The writings of Moses bear witness to this, for they contain words that are coarse and unworthy of the uncircumscribed God. Moses did not set these words out on his own account; God proclaimed them through his angels on Mount Sinai, at the tent. Because an angel spoke them, Moses did not put his name in the record of them at all, as the other prophets did in the books of their own prophecies. — By "eyelids" [you are to understand] his judging providence, which examines all affairs.
v. 5. But he who loves injustice hates his own soul.
If he who loves injustice hates his own soul, then clearly he who hates injustice loves his own soul.
v. 6. Fire and brimstone and a stormy wind are the portion of their cup.
Here he calls punishment a cup, in which the drink of wickedness and ignorance has been mixed.
v. 1. Save me, Lord, for the godly one has failed, for truths have dwindled from among the sons of men. Vatic. p. 690, 1.

Since the gift of truth is in danger of being extinguished, the godly have failed and truths have dwindled. Truths are found not only among the godly; godliness is also found among the truthful. Or else: because the godly have failed, truths have dwindled for that reason. Perhaps the scarcity of the godly has been the cause of the many heresies.
v. 6. Because of the misery of the poor and the groaning of the needy, now I will arise, says the Lord; I will set him in safety; I will speak boldly in it.

"If because of the misery of the poor I will now arise," he says, says the Lord, then who does not fear the Lord when he arises? And again: "Arise, O Lord my God, be exalted." Let us pray to be spared such an exaltation, and let us not wish to see his hand raised against the disobedient, still less let loose upon the harder-hearted. And he did not forget the cry of the poor, and the poor man will not be forgotten for ever. Or it may be read this way: "The poor, who have become poor for my sake and needy in your spirit, are always groaning as they are humbled. They attend to my word and keep their faith unwavering. For their sake I will arise, and, as is fitting, by my rising I will establish salvation for all people."
v. 8, 9. You, Lord, will guard us and preserve us... The ungodly walk round in a circle.

A circle is the opposite of a straight line, as crookedness is the opposite of straightness. Since the ungodly walk in a circle, the godly must walk a straight path. That is why he says, "You will guard us": the ungodly encircle us and close us in, plotting against our salvation. These would be the opposing powers.
v. 1. For the end; a psalm of David.

Argument, by Eusebius. For the sake of the end, the one that is with God, he fought manfully through everything that comes before the end. The end is the fruit of one's labours, and it brings eternal life and the kingdom of heaven to those who contend genuinely. Since David too was one of these, he sent up the psalm and the song to God "for the end". But at the beginning, as one still in the contest, he uttered the first words:
v. 2. How long, Lord, will you forget me, to the end? How long will you turn your face away from me? Vatic. p. 650, 2.

By the same. He teaches that at a certain time he had fallen out of God's remembrance [into forgetfulness]. (God forgets those who forget him, and everyone who sins forgets him.) God also turns his face away from those who do something shameful, unworthy of his eyes, that is, of his power to behold and oversee. So, living in great concern about God's judgement and anguished over what he knew about himself, struck by his conscience and pained in soul by his thoughts, he goes on:
v. 3. How long shall I take counsel in my soul, with grief in my heart day and night?

By the same. Symmachus translated this as: "Anxiety in my mind every day." These things, he says, were written for our admonition. If we ever need repentance and confession for things we have not done rightly, we too should take on the disposition of the one who said these words and use the same methods, like saving medicines for the soul, making timely use of these words of confession.
v. 1. They are corrupt and have become abominable in their practices. Vatic. p. 650, 2.

"When I came," says the Lord, "I found not a single worker of goodness, but each one guilty of every outrageous deed." If they are corrupted in their practices, then perhaps it is not the base thought that corrupts, but the actual carrying out of that thought.
v. 3. And they have not known the way of peace; there is no fear of God before their eyes.
"I am the way," says the Saviour, and he himself is our peace. — For by the fear of the Lord everyone turns away from evil.
v. 4. Those who devour my people as they eat bread.
When evildoers drew near against me to eat my flesh.
v. 6. You have put to shame the counsel of the poor man, but the Lord is his hope.
For the Lord became poor for our sake, though he was rich, so that by his poverty we might become rich.
v. 3. And he has not taken up a reproach against his neighbours. Vatic. p. 691, 1.
He who lives blamelessly does not take up a reproach against his neighbours.
v. 5. He has not lent his money at interest.
This must be said to moneylenders, as something that bars them from dwelling on the holy mountain.
Ibid. He who does these things will never be shaken.

Eusebius. Whoever has accomplished all the things listed above together has become complete [?]. He has kept the whole body of the godly way of life entire, sound as it were and perfected in every good word and deed, and he will never be shaken.
v. 4. I will not gather their assemblies from blood, nor will I mention their names with my lips. Vat. 691, 2.

"When I gather assemblies from the nations," he says, "I will not gather them through blood, nor will I have them approach me through the worship of the law, but rather through praise and the bloodless sacrifice. In the past," he says, "they bore names that matched their deeds and were called idolaters and polytheists. But now I will no longer mention those names." Instead he calls them godly and holy, called and elect.
v. 9. And my tongue rejoiced.
Here he calls the gift of the Spirit a tongue.
v. 3. You have tested my heart; you visited it by night.

Affliction produces endurance, and endurance produces testing, so affliction produces testing. And if the testing took place at night, then night here signifies affliction, in which the rational soul stumbles and is darkened. — "Enter through the narrow gate and the afflicted way", that is, the practical life. At first it seems to bring pain rather than joy, but later it yields fruits of righteousness to those who have been trained by it.
v. 7. Make your mercies wonderful, you who save those who hope in you; from those who resist your right hand guard me as the apple of your eye.

Job calls the power that struck him the hand of God: "It is your hand," he says; "let it not whirl me about so." In the same way David calls the enemies of God's beneficent hand the sword of God. God's beneficent hand is the angels, through whom he provides for the sensible world. The angels want all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth, and the demons oppose them.
v. 9. Smoke went up in his wrath, and fire blazed from his face; coals were kindled by it. Vat. 632, 2.

He was angered, he says, and cast down the fire, and with it he set men ablaze in turn. The coals are the company of the apostles. On the day of Pentecost they partook of this fire and received tongues of fire upon their heads, so they were fittingly called coals, for they both enlightened and purified the nations. Learn from what follows that these things took place:
v. 10, 11. And he bowed the heavens and came down, and thick darkness was under his feet; and he mounted upon the cherubim. Sic Vat. 633, 1.
"Cherubim" is interpreted as "knowledge and understanding", so he is speaking of the righteous.
v. 12. And he made darkness his hiding place; round about him was his tent.

He made darkness his hiding place and set it between himself and us, just as Moses long ago set the veil between himself and the hardness of Israel. This was so that a darkened nature might not easily see [?] and gain that hidden beauty, since what is easily gained is easily thrown away because it was easy to acquire. That is why this bodily darkness stands between us and God, as the cloud once stood between the Egyptians and the Hebrews. This is perhaps what is meant by "he made darkness his hiding place." That is also why Paul says: "who alone has immortality and dwells in unapproachable light."
v. 20. He will rescue me, because he desired me.
Rescued in this way by your providence, I hope to overcome all my foes, and not to stop until I have made them subject again. He indicated this as well when he said: "They will fall beneath my feet."
v. 36. And your discipline, etc.
"And your discipline itself will teach me" is Theodotion's rendering. It stands in place of "And your discipline set me upright to the end", which is the reading of the Seventy.
v. 40. You hobbled beneath me all who rose up against me.
Yet we do not know of David reigning over his enemies. So the prophecy is fulfilled through the one born of him according to the flesh.
v. 41. And you made my enemies turn their backs to me.
That is: you put them to flight. For turning one's back is what those who flee do.
v. 49. My deliverer from wrathful enemies.

In those whom rage dominates, wrathfulness is also found. If our enemies are wrathful, then our enemies are full of rage. For "their rage," it says, "is like the serpent's," and "when his rage was kindled in wrath against us."
v. 3, 4. Day pours forth speech to day, and night proclaims knowledge to night. There are no speeches or words whose voices are not heard. Vatic. p. 634, 2.

Eusebius. Night and day are fixed measures that give way to each other in due season as they decrease and increase, and they always keep the same proportion to each other. By their works they proclaim the one who set both in place. Constancy and freedom from confusion are not found in things that happen by chance; harmony is the offspring of wisdom. And the voices of their words are not among those that go unheard, for they are heard everywhere in the world through the sight of the heavens, which are seen both night and day. Paul applied these words to the apostles. That is why he quoted them without naming the source, and not as he usually does in the preceding passages: "But Isaiah cries out concerning Israel." And again: "As Isaiah foretold." And again: "As it is written." And again: "For the scripture says." Symmachus rendered it more clearly: "And night proclaims knowledge to night, not by utterances nor by words whose voices are not heard; rather, their sound has gone out into all the earth." Or, according to Aquila: "Their measuring line." For they utter neither word nor voice, but by displaying their rule and their proper order they summon all land and sea to the divine hymn of praise. — The day of the resurrection pours forth speech to the day of the cross: how the one crucified on that day rose on this day as God and raised the dead. And the night that came before the cross proclaims this knowledge to the night of Christ's betrayal: how on that night he was afraid and prayed and afterward was even betrayed, while on this night he has been shown to be master of the elements, so that he even brought night upon the middle of the day.
v. 6. In the sun he has set his tent, and he, like a bridegroom coming out of his chamber, will rejoice like a giant to run his course. Athanasius.

He called the Virgin a bridal chamber, from whom Christ the bridegroom came forth. He was pure of every stain, since he came out of a pure bridal chamber. The holy Virgin is Christ's bridal chamber because she gave birth without a man, and so she fittingly had as her bridegroom the very one born of her, who brought about the birth by invisible power. — "Giant" is interpreted as "one who falls upon", and it is understood of the Lord. He rejoiced at the time of the dispensation as he worked out our salvation, and he fell upon the battle lines of the demons and abolished their dominion over us. Understand the "course" as the Lord's becoming man, in which he ran rejoicing like a giant because of the strength he displayed on the cross and in death. In the same way he rejoiced in the Gospel over finding the one sheep. He left the ninety-nine sheep that had not strayed, that is, the angelic powers, on the mountains, that is, in the heavens. He went after the sheep that had strayed, and when he found it he rejoiced. Or else he ran the road to the heavens rejoicing, or he ran from earth to the regions under the earth.
v. 8. The law of the Lord is blameless, converting souls.

Origen. We must ask whether it converts from vice to virtue or from sensible things to intelligible ones. Perhaps it is the second, for the first is what the commandment naturally does. By "law" he clearly means the law of the Gospel. The gentiles had already been schooled by the elements mentioned above to know that there is one creator, and next they are taught the law of the Gospel too, since it converted the souls of all the nations to the truth. — Because of his boundless love for us, he does not pass by the fornicator or the robber, even those who have fled far from his love and reached the very depths of sin.
v. 10. The judgements of the Lord are true, justified altogether.

He had to add the third verse to the two before it. God's judgements are fearful to sinners and transgressors, something to be shunned [?]. But to those who do and keep God's law they are more precious than any wealth, because of the hope of reward, and they even seem sweeter than any pleasure.
v. 12. For your servant indeed keeps them; in keeping them there is great reward.

This too has been clearly shown to us in the preceding psalm. They are called true and righteous, justified by the true God and righteous judge. "Altogether" means "on the same account": for the reason they are true is the same reason they are also righteous. — If your servant keeps them, then whoever does not keep them is not your servant. And the one who keeps what God desires is the one who desires nothing other than these things. Therefore he has a great reward among the things that are to come from God.
v. 13, 14. Who will understand his transgressions? Cleanse me from my hidden faults, and spare your servant from alien things.

Aquila rendered it "of arrogant strangers." This passion sometimes attends those who are succeeding, when the mind grows slack over its success, and so they are thrown headlong once more in another way. The apostle speaks of this: "lest, being puffed up, he fall into the condemnation of the devil." Having first said, as he had to, "For your servant keeps them," he begs to be delivered from pride. Once he has been cleansed of it, since it is a great sin, "I shall be blameless of pride," having been cleansed of hidden faults at the same time. For now I do not yet have confidence.
vv. 3–4. May he send you help from the sanctuary, and support you from Zion. May he remember every sacrifice of yours, and may your whole burnt offering be made fat. Vatic. p. 635, 1.

He will deliver you, he says, as you offer him a spiritual sacrifice in thanksgiving. The word "every" points to a great number, for he does not remember a small one. A whole burnt offering is made fat when it is given over wholly to the spiritual fire, which is the Spirit. This will happen when those who offer it are spiritual.
v. 8. Some trust in chariots and some in horses.
Understand the horses as the wild prancing of the passions, which the demons mount. The chariots are the impulsive passions joined together, and in these the demons equip themselves against us.
v. 10. O Lord, save your king, and hear us.
For the present, save for us our king, David.
v. 7. For you will give him blessing for ever and ever; you will gladden him with joy in your presence. Vatic. p. 635, 2.

He says to him, "Come, blessed of my Father." Grace and peace are given from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ, and in the same way blessing is given from God and from his face. The face of God is the imprint of his substance. With him the king rejoices, offering a foretaste of the things hoped for. Or else the king, having become [?] the temple of God the Word, the Image, is called his temple, and rejoices because he has been conformed to him.
v. 9. May your hand be found by all your enemies; may your right hand find all who hate you.
It is a benefit to be rid of sins and evil thoughts, for an evil thought is the seed of sin.
v. 4. But you dwell in the sanctuary, O praise of Israel. Vatic. p. 636, 1.
From this we learn that the Lord is praise itself. He is praised by Israel, while he himself is praise.
v. 7. But I am a worm.
He speaks as in the person of God incarnate. The words "I am the worm" are not taken in respect of his divinity, but in respect of what was seen and of the lowliness of the flesh.
v. 19. They looked closely and gazed at me.
They were probably feeling his whole body and measuring each of the bones, to see where the nails should be driven.
v. 21. Deliver my soul from the sword.
Simeon too says to the holy Mother of God: "And a sword will pierce your own soul as well."
And my only one from the hand of the dog.

He now uses the singular, naming by their kind those he earlier called "dogs." — He called his own soul "only one" because it alone did not know sin, and also because it alone was united with God the Word at all times. Perhaps he calls the church that is presented to him "only one," since she has no spot or wrinkle and is made up entirely of the blameless. According to their progress, these are divided into different ranks [?]: "There are sixty queens and eighty concubines, and maidens without number; but above them all is the perfect dove," the only one of her mother, the Jerusalem above.
vv. 1–2. The Lord shepherds me, and I shall lack nothing. In a place of green pasture, there he has made me camp; beside the water of rest he has nourished me. Vatic. p. 637, 1.

The perfect person is the one recognized as being in the image and likeness of God. The Lord is called his king, but not his shepherd. The one making progress in the early stages may be called a sheep of God. He is shepherded by God and feeds on the gospel. He drinks the water that leaves the drinker thirsting no more, but not yet the wine of the true vine. He finds rest through the washing of regeneration, setting down the burden of his sins. In another sense, whoever has attained the gentleness and steadiness of Christ is shepherded by him onto the green pasture, which is moral teaching. "In it he has made me camp," he says, not "made me settle." Elsewhere he says, "He will shepherd us forever." Consider and understand the green pasture, its spiritual place, and the spiritual water of rest. These are given to the one who is still being shepherded, until he becomes able to share in the rational table and the cup. If any of the letter does not yet kill, that will be the green pasture. But for those who are shepherded spiritually, a table is prepared for those who endure afflictions.
v. 3. He has restored my soul; he has led me in paths of righteousness for his name's sake.

Like the shepherd, he went ahead and wore down paths beforehand, so that his own sheep could follow in his footsteps. Righteousness is the practical disposition of the righteous, and its paths are its activities. If someone takes righteousness to mean virtue in general, he will say its paths are the particular virtues. The Lord leads to these whoever bears his name. "He has restored my soul," he says, meaning the soul that had wandered from its own or had fallen. Or the Lord turns back the soul that has fallen away and restores it after shepherding it, and it camps in a place of green pasture. Then, having turned it back, he leads it onto paths of righteousness and virtue.
v. 4. For even if I walk in the midst of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil.

You might also take "shadow of death" to mean natural and common death, as distinct from the death of the soul. In that sense it is said that the soul that sins shall die, and that whoever believes in the Son of God will never die, because he has passed from death into life. For such people do not submit to [?] the shadow of death, whether dangers or the dissolution of the body.
v. 5. You have prepared a table before me in the face of those who afflict me; you have anointed my head with oil, and your cup that makes drunk, how excellent it is!

What does "in the face of those who afflict me" mean? It holds an unspeakable mystery, such that one might even pray to be afflicted. Think of the great games, where prizes are set for each event. The same is true of each affliction. Whenever something afflicting is present, together with the afflicting and hostile powers, understand that a spiritual and intelligible table has been prepared because of that affliction. As often as you are afflicted, so often is a spiritual table set before you. Only have eyes that see my tables, so that you may give thanks and say with the apostle: "And not only that, but we also boast in our afflictions." At the beginning we said that the one who is making progress camps in a place of green pasture. When he reaches the end, he no longer remains a sheep but has been shown to be rational, and so he has a table of rational foods prepared by the Lord... Consider also this: as long as a person is in this life, seeing through a mirror and in a riddle, he is a sheep led by a shepherd. But when he passes into the age to come and meets the truth face to face, he comes to a spiritual table, as it is written: "And I will make a covenant with you, to eat and drink at my Father's table in the truth." That is why it says "you have prepared," for from this world on God has prepared "what eye has not seen," and so on. "Before me" shows that the table has been revealed and made known to me "in the face of those who afflict me," since many wish to be my enemies. The Lord wants me to stand firm against those who afflict me, and so he has prepared a table before me with solid food laid on it. Filled with it like an athlete, I may be able to resist my afflicters nobly. For when we attain perfect goods, our adversaries are stronger and more numerous, as the apostle says: "For a great door has opened to me, and there are many adversaries." — The person whose head is anointed with oil by the Lord will say, "Let not the oil of a sinner anoint my head," just as Christ is anointed by God with the oil of gladness. I also think that whoever fasts in this way anoints his head and washes his face. — And since not only a table, etc.
v. 6. And your mercy will pursue me all the days of my life, and I shall dwell in the house of the Lord for length of days.

Who is the mercy that pursues? I learned from the apostle that Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God, and that he became for us wisdom from God, and righteousness, sanctification and redemption. He himself says, "I am the way and the life and the truth." Learn that he is also the mercy that pursues. A living mercy pursues you. He overtakes and seizes those who flee less, and leads them into the church, so that he may have mercy on them. They may then dwell in the house of the Lord for length of days, and in the holy church in heaven, and become long-lived.
v. 1. The earth is the Lord's and all that fills it, the world and all who dwell in it. Vatic. p. 637, 2.
He means the world in which he rejoiced when he had finished making it.
v. 4. Innocent of hands and pure in heart.

We have often spoken about the lifting up of hands. Moses lifted up his hands and Israel prevailed, but when he let his hands down, Amalek prevailed. It is also written, "lifting up holy hands without anger or disputing," and "The lifting up of my hands is an evening sacrifice." I would therefore say that our hands are our deeds done in godliness. If we store up treasure in heaven, our hands are lifted up to God and we conquer the enemy. But when our hands drop down, we cannot avoid being conquered. So when I lift up my hands to God, and through the hands of the soul am raised up to him, Amalek is conquered by me and is nowhere to be found. We must therefore lift up our hands toward God's holy temple, and the temple of God is the glory of God. BB. 637.
v. 10. Who is this King of glory? The Lord, mighty and powerful, the Lord of hosts.

The title "Almighty" may fittingly be applied to the Savior. All things came into being through him, he is before all things, and all things hold together in him. He rules by his providence over everything that came into being through him, and he is before everything that holds together in him. It follows that he is called Almighty. Indeed, it is he who speaks in Zechariah: "Thus says the Lord Almighty: After glory he has sent me... and you will know that the Lord Almighty has sent me to you." For the Son is the Almighty sent by the Almighty, sent by the Father. Most clearly of all, the Savior is called Almighty in the Revelation of John: "Thus says the Lord, the faithful and true witness, who was and who is and who is to come, the Lord, God the Almighty." Beyond dispute, these words are spoken about the Son.
v. 4. Remember your compassions. Vatic. p. 638, 1.
For whatever kind of person someone may be, he needs mercy from God.
v. 19. See my enemies, how many they have become; they have hated me with an unjust hatred.
Those who hate the righteous for being righteous hate them with an unjust hatred.
v. 21. The innocent and upright clung to me, because I waited for you, O Lord.

You might also give "innocent" and "upright" other meanings. The innocent could be those who are free of wickedness, or the simpler people, and the upright could be the perfect. Or the innocent could be those from among humans, and the upright the angels above them.
v. 4. I have not sat with the council of vanity, and I will not go in with lawbreakers. Vatic. p. 638, 2.
These words should be spoken to those who watch horse races and theatrical shows, and also to those who have become partners in heresies.
v. 8. O Lord, I have loved the beauty of your house, and the place where your glory dwells.
The Lord's place is peace of soul. For, it says, "his place came to be in peace."
v. 11. But I have walked in my innocence.
These words are spoken by someone who eagerly keeps his soul free from passion.
